---
title: "Appendix 2 — The applicability downgrade: easy absences inflate reported skill"
date: last-modified
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 150)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(data.table); library(ggplot2)})
HERE <- ".." # this .qmd lives in manuscript/; repo root is ..
for (f in list.files(file.path(HERE, "R"), "^fn_.*\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)
```

**Situation.** A reported PR-AUC or ROC-AUC summarises a model over its whole test set. 
However, the ease of far-away absences of pseudo-absences is likely to increase these reported metrics in the areas of landscape most difficult to distinguish suitable habitat in. 
How does restricting the analysis to the area of applicability affect PR-AUC and ROC-AUC scores? 

**Experiment.** We computed the Area of Applicability from the **training presences only** (pseudo-absences conflate the dissimilarity index) and labelled every hold-out point interpolation (`DI ≤ DI_thresh`) or extrapolation (`DI > DI_thresh`). 
This split is nearly collinear with the outcome: presences and a few hard absences fall in-domain, while the great majority of absences, environmentally distant from any occurrence, fall out-of-domain. 
We then scored each model two ways: *naive*, on the full hold-out, and *AOA-honest*, on the in-domain points only, reweighting both to the same prevalence so the only difference is which absences are considered. 
Performance was compared with ROC-AUC (prevalence-invariant) across all 128 SDM models.

{{< include _aoa_downgrade.qmd >}}

**Result.** Restricting to the in-domain region, where the model must separate presences from absences that *resemble* occupied habitat, lowers measured skill in **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", pct_drop)` of `r n_models` models** (median ROC-AUC `r sprintf("%.2f", med_full)` -> `r sprintf("%.2f", med_in)`). 
The headline number is inflated by free credit for trivially rejecting the easy, far-from-suitable extrapolation absences. 
In decision terms the effect is stark: the naive curve looks uniformly excellent, while the honest curve loses all value beyond a threshold of ~10%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aoa-inflation
#| fig-cap: "Naive vs AOA-honest decision curve for the example model, both at 5% prevalence. The two agree only at the broadest thresholds; the gap is the inflation contributed by easy absences, and the in-domain curve drops below \"survey none\" well before the \"survey five to find one\" tolerance."
p_aoa
```

**Isolating it from ground truth.** This downgrade uses only the hold-out predictions and the presences-only dissimilarity index, hence an *a priori*, quantified penalty.
Further it is orthogonal to the prevalence correction of Appendix 1 (that sets the baseline; this measures discrimination among the hard cases). 
What it cannot reach is the *other* edge: the hold-out contains almost no points in genuinely novel, high-suitability environments, so it cannot characterise dangerous extrapolation. 
As expected, models perform poorly when extrapolating beyond their training space, but quantifying *that* collapse is an a posteriori, ground-truth question, not something the hold-out can answer.

**Conclusion.** Report model skill restricted to the area of applicability; the headline, whole-test number overstates decision-relevant performance, and the overstatement is computable before any field work.
